description: participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
NASA has detected fires from orbit with MODIS since 2002 and with the sharper VIIRS instrument since 2012. VIIRS records about 2.75 times as many active fire cells over Argentina, so joining the two records creates a false 2.24× jump in 2012 that distorts every trend and anomaly crossing that year.

Hotspot Observatory builds one consistent fire record for Argentina from January 2003 to October 2026. We calibrated MODIS to the VIIRS scale on the years both satellites flew, chose among four competing models using years held out of fitting, and cut monthly error against VIIRS from 66% to 12%. The 2012 seam now changes by 0.89× instead of 2.24×.

The record powers an interactive tool for researchers studying when and where fire seasons peak, monitoring teams asking whether this month is unusual, and agencies deciding where to focus. Users pick any area, step through 286 months on a map, compare seasons and trends, and export results. Every value shows whether it was observed or estimated, with its uncertainty.
details:
What it does

NASA's two fire-detecting instruments can't simply be joined. MODIS (Aqua satellite, about 1 km pixels, since 2002) misses many fires that VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, 375 m pixels, since 2012) detects. Over Argentina, VIIRS records about 2.75 times as many active fire cells. A record that uses MODIS before 2012 and VIIRS after shows a false 2.24× jump in 2012, which distorts every trend, anomaly and seasonal comparison that crosses that year.

Hotspot Observatory delivers two things:

  1. A harmonized fire record: one monthly series of satellite-detected fire activity for Argentina, January 2003 to October 2026, on the VIIRS scale, at 0.1° resolution, for daytime and nighttime passes.
    • a map of active 0.1° cells for the selected month;
    • a monthly timeline used to step through 286 months;
    • a year-by-month fire calendar;
    • seasonal comparisons against recent seasons;
    • long-term trends with a statistical test;
    • seasonal profiles for four regions;
    • a side-by-side view of the two raw instruments.

How it works

  1. A comparable unit. We count active cell-days: a 0.1° grid cell scores one for each day an instrument detected fire in it, counted separately for each instrument. Counting cells rather than raw detections removes most of the pixel-size difference. We chose this unit after a diagnostic comparison of both sensors.
  2. Competing hypotheses. We fitted four calibration models on 2012–2019, when both satellites flew: a constant ratio, a power law, a power law with monthly terms, and a power law for each 2° block.
    • monthly error (MAPE) 12.4%, against 65.7% for raw MODIS and 16.0% for a constant ratio;
    • monthly R² 0.97;
    • annual error 6.4%.
  3. Measured uncertainty. 80% prediction intervals come from leave-one-year-out refits. We measured their real coverage on held-out months and report it: 70%, below the nominal 80%.
  4. Building the record. Observed VIIRS is used wherever it exists. MODIS is converted only for 2003–2011 and for five months when VIIRS was offline. Outages are detected automatically, and 2026 outages were confirmed by checking that the satellite returned no data anywhere in the world before any month was filled. At the 2012 seam, observed VIIRS differs from the model by only +0.04%.

Benefits

  • Trustworthy long-term comparisons. Users can compare 2005 with 2025 on one scale without the false 2012 jump.
  • Honest about every number. Each value is labelled observed, back-cast, gap-filled, incomplete or provisional. Comparisons that would rely on incomplete data are withheld instead of shown.
  • Answers questions directly. "Is this August unusual?" gives a value, median, rank and percentile class in one place.
  • Reproducible. Every parameter is downloadable, and the pipeline refuses to publish unless it reproduces the validated coefficients and scores.
  • Accessible. Colourblind-safe palettes, keyboard operation, screen-reader labels and a layout that works on phones.

Intended impact

  • Fire-season analysis (climate scientists, fire researchers, environmental agencies): when and where activity peaks, and whether that is changing. For example, Patagonia's season peaks in February while northern Argentina peaks in August.
  • Anomaly detection (fire analysts, monitoring agencies, early-warning teams): whether a month is unusual. For example, August 2020 was 58% above the historical August median nationally, the second highest of 18 Augusts. The tool states that an anomaly is a signal to investigate, not a prediction of fire.
  • Regional fire-risk research (emergency-response agencies, fire managers, climate modellers): which areas are persistently active and when, exported with full provenance to combine with fire-weather and climate data.

How it is creative

  • We treated harmonization as a scientific experiment, not a fixed conversion factor: competing models, a held-out test, and a published comparison of all four.
  • We confirm satellite outages against worldwide records before filling any data, so a quiet fire day is never mistaken for a missing one.
  • The tool checks its own uncertainty: it rebuilds the prediction intervals and shows them only if they reproduce the reported coverage.
  • Quality-aware analysis: every comparison knows whether its inputs are complete and withholds results that would mislead.
  • A workspace where map, timeline, calendar and inspector stay linked to one area and one month, and the whole state fits in a shareable link.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity over convenience. We publish limitations inside the tool: validation is national, so regional accuracy is not yet independently measured; from 2023 the Aqua satellite's later overpass makes the model over-predict by about 12%; and intervals are narrower than nominal.
  • Avoiding misreading. Active cell-days are not fire counts or burned area, and the tool explains this beside every headline number.
  • Data quality and latency. Near-real-time months are labelled provisional; incomplete months are flagged, never treated as zero.
  • Scope. We focused on Argentina to validate the method properly before extending it. Each new country needs its own calibration and validation.
    • regional validation;
    • drift-aware recalibration;
    • recalibrated interval width;
    • province-level areas;
    • automated updates;
    • other countries.

Tools and software

  • Science pipeline: Python with pandas, NumPy, PyArrow and Matplotlib.
  • API: FastAPI.
  • Interface: React, Vite, MapLibre GL and hand-built SVG charts.
  • Testing: pytest, Node's test runner and Playwright. 90 backend, 23 unit and 30 end-to-end tests check that every displayed number traces to the data.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2 active-fire archives and the FIRMS API; Natural Earth boundaries; OpenStreetMap basemap.
  • Hardware: none needed. It runs in any modern browser.

Use of AI

All of the code in this project was generated with AI coding assistants, under our direction. Our team defined the challenge approach: put both instruments on one scale by calibrating MODIS against VIIRS on the years both satellites flew, and test the calibration on held-out years it was not fitted to. We chose the use cases, specified what to build, reviewed the outputs, and checked results against NASA FIRMS data. OpenAI Codex implemented the data-processing and calibration pipeline. Claude (Anthropic) implemented the API, the web application and the automated tests. The processed datasets in the repository were produced by this AI-generated code. Every number shown in the tool is computed from NASA FIRMS data, and automated tests check displayed values against the underlying data.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System)
MODIS Collection 6.1 Active Fire Detections (MCD14ML), Aqua, standard processing, 2003–2025, from FIRMS yearly country archives
VIIRS 375 m Active Fire Detections, Collection 2 (VNP14IMGML), Suomi-NPP, standard processing, 2012–2025, from FIRMS yearly country archives
FIRMS Area API: 2026 MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP standard and near-real-time detections
FIRMS Data Availability API (choosing standard or near-real-time data for each sensor)
MODIS Terra and VIIRS NOAA-20 active fire data via FIRMS (used only to confirm satellite outages)
